title: Rectify adaptive batch fairness under tenant microbursts to prevent queue-starvation and long-context tail latency
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Summary: Multiple customers across Hosted and Dedicated reported sudden tail-latency spikes and throughput drops during high short-request microbursts when long-context requests were present. Symptoms included queue starvation for latency-sensitive short requests, elevated 95/99th latency on routes with mixed context lengths, and degraded KV-cache hit rates leading to sustained long-context tail.

Repro: We reproduced with a synthetic workload that interleaves frequent short completions (<=64 tokens) at bursty arrival rates and a few concurrent long-context generation requests (>8k tokens). Under the adaptive batching/scheduling path, the scheduler forms heterogeneous batches which then get dominated by long requests because of KV cache eviction and preemption behavior. This causes head-of-line and queue amplification for short requests.

Root cause hypotheses and confirmation:
- Scheduler's adaptive batch growth policy prioritizes batch fill over latency fairness; when bursts arrive it binds slots to an existing long-request batch to avoid kernel churn. Confirmed by trace logs and batch histograms.
- KV cache eviction policy interacts poorly with mixed-length workloads: long requests keep large KV allocations causing eviction of hot prefixes used by many short requests. Confirmed by eviction counters correlating with latency spikes.
- Preemptive tenant fairness (recent rollout) had a regression where preemption windows were too coarse, allowing long requests to block short request admission for 200-800ms. Reproduced with canary toggles.

Proposed fix plan:
1) Fast mitigation (hotfix, today): introduce a small short-request priority lane that bypasses batch growth heuristics when observed short-request ratio > 50% in the last 1s window. This is a scheduler config gate and will ship to Hosted first.
2) Mid-term (next 2 sprints): refine adaptive batch scoring to weigh latency sensitivity and estimated KV residency. Add a penalty for batches with heterogeneous length mixes that predicts eviction churn.
3) KV cache improvement (investigation ongoing): implement LRU aging that accounts for request frequency and prefix reuse, and cap per-tenant KV footprint to prevent eviction storms.
4) Preemption tuning: reduce preemption granularity and add a fast-preempt path for requests under size threshold to ensure admission within 50ms.

Rollout strategy:
- Canary on Hosted canary region for 24h with synthetic workload and customer traffic mirror.
- Staged rollout to Hosted, then Dedicated pools that opt-in; Private customers get a config patch and recommendation notes.
- Monitor p95/p99, KV eviction rate, batch size distribution, and request admission lag. Automated rollback if p99 increases by >15% vs baseline.

Monitoring & Alerts:
- New dashboards: "scheduler-adaptive-batch-mix" and "kv-eviction-by-tenant".
- Alert thresholds: p99 latency jump of +10% (pager), kv-eviction rate > 200/s sustained for 30s (pager), admission-lag > 100ms (ops notify).

Customer communications:
- Drafted incident note and proposed remediation for impacted customers. PM to coordinate RFO and follow-up runbook.

Open questions / trade-offs:
- Aggressive short-request bias reduces throughput efficiency for long-batch workloads; trade against cost. We'll gate via runtime config and A/B tests.
- Per-tenant KV caps may penalize heavy long-request workloads; need quota model and SLO alignment.

Artifacts and links:
- Repro harness and traces: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/tree/main/tests/bench/adaptive-burst-repro
- Design doc: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/INF/Adaptive+Batching+Fairness+RFC
- PR for hotfix: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/5421
- KV telemetry dashboard (prototype): https://dashboard.redwood.ai/d/kv-ops/kv-eviction-by-tenant

Acceptance criteria:
- p99 on mixed workloads down to within 5% of baseline across Hosted canary and Dedicated opt-in pools under identical synthetic load.
- KV eviction rate reduced by >=40% during bursts in experiments.
- No regression to throughput beyond 7% for long-request heavy workloads.

Follow-ups:
- Postmortem once stable with customer impact timeline and persistent mitigations.
- Product review to determine if we should expose "latency-sensitive" route hints in public API for customers to opt-in.
